source.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful for Java Function Bug Detection?
source.authors: M. Rui; Cláudia Mamede; Andre Catarino; Rui Abreu; Henrique Lopes Cardoso

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present and usable, though some PDF-extracted equations and layout are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: Applies pretrained SAEs to a new setting—Java bug detection—and reports how well classifiers using their features perform. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: Reports SAE-feature classification results, token-level activation case studies, and feature-importance results. The layer-wise and transfer plots are described, but most plotted values are not available in the supplied text. Background claims and cited results are not treated as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: Pretrained SAEs (Bloom GPT-2 Small, Gemma Scope) serve only as feature extractors. The study reports how well Random Forests trained on top-K SAE latents detect Java bugs, compared with TF-IDF and fine-tuned encoder baselines. It never tests whether features are superposed or whether the dictionary recovers the model's features (no reconstruction or feature-recovery result, no random or untrained control). It also does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical, nor their dimensionality. Classification accuracy of its own pipeline is method performance, not evidence for V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SAE-derived features from frozen GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2B, with simple Random Forests, detect Java bugs (F1 up to 0.89) and can outperform fine-tuned GraphCodeBERT/ModernBERT. They add that Gemma features are more discriminative and transfer more consistently. They caution, citing Heap et al., that the features may reflect superficial patterns rather than learned semantics, and that binary classification may overstate semantic alignment. Note that the abstract's 'without task-specific supervision' is inaccurate: feature selection and the classifiers use labelled buggy/patched pairs.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses pretrained residual-stream SAEs and Random Forest classification for Java bug detection; it does not implement toy-model feature-overlap, sparsity-transition, or interference measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by model, dataset, and transfer setting: Gemma 2B leads on the stated Github-Bug Java and HumanEval results; GPT-2 Small has the stated Defects4J result and greater reported degradation transferring to HumanEval. Layer-wise analysis is conducted, but detailed layer-specific values are not present in the supplied text.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-K SAE latents from frozen GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2B, fed to Random Forests, classify buggy vs patched Java functions with F1 up to 0.89. The authors report this outperforms fine-tuned encoder baselines, with no uncertainty reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents from pretrained LLMs carry linearly selectable signal useful for downstream code-bug classification.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the stated performance values. The supplied text lacks most numerical results from the figures. The authors themselves note that SAE features may reflect superficial input patterns or architectural biases, that binary classification may overstate semantic alignment, and that SAE training has non-trivial cost. No untrained-model or random-feature control is reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper describes layer-wise classification heatmaps (Figure 8) and transfer results (Figure 10), but most plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text. No additional rows were extracted from those plots beyond the textual transfer finding in r9.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.

No measurement of features spread across neurons. No test that SAEs recover genuine sparse features (reconstruction, untrained-model or random-dictionary controls). The authors only cite Heap et al. on this point.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with V4 supports is overturned. This is an application paper using SAEs as a tool, and all rows are own-method performance or illustrative case studies. The text gives no baseline numbers, no uncertainty, and no untrained or random-feature control. Layer-wise (Fig. 8) and transfer (Fig. 10) values are not in the text. Even if extracted, they would not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, interference measurement, or regular geometry test.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by competition for representational capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

Tests whether pretrained SAE features from two LLMs support Java bug classification and reports illustrative feature activations. It does not establish that LLM features generally spread across neurons, or that the recovered features are robust or semantically complete.
Does not test completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
